items.text: Burnout doesn't take your skills. It takes your *access* to them. When the words stop or the familiar route goes blank — the ability is still there. The bandwidth isn't. That's a different problem with a different solution.
items.rationale: Names the regression/access distinction head-on. 'Regression' implies permanent decline; the reframe converts fear into accurate understanding and points toward the right intervention: reduce load, not alarm.

items.text: 'Regression' implies you went backwards. Burnout means the route is blocked. The destination hasn't moved — and neither have you.
items.rationale: Tighter, single-metaphor take on the same angle — different enough from post 1 to run separately. The 'neither have you' close lands the reassurance without sentimentality.

items.text: Autistic women often seek a first assessment during perimenopause. Not because something new is happening — because estrogen withdrawal depletes the cognitive resources that powered masking for decades.
items.rationale: Names the specific mechanism behind midlife first-diagnosis without pathologizing it. 'Often' is accurate and non-totalizing. Reframes 'falling apart in midlife' as a systems-capacity story.
items.sensitivity_flag: References a hormonal mechanism (estrogen withdrawal → cognitive depletion) drawn from Frontiers in Reproductive Health 2026 and Psychology Today Apr 2026 — defensible, but confirm the phrasing doesn't read as medical advice or treatment claim before posting.

items.text: In PDA, anxiety isn't the engine — it's the exhaust. If you treat anxiety without reducing demands, you're fixing the smoke alarm while the fire runs.
items.rationale: One crisp analogy does the heavy lifting. Speaks directly to parents and clinicians who've tried anxiety-first interventions without results. No prescription — the implication is structural.

items.text: A 2026 study found sensory over-reactivity predicts demand avoidance in PDA kids even after controlling for anxiety. The sensory load is upstream. Anxiety is downstream. That order matters.
items.rationale: Leads with the data, distills the implication without prescribing treatment. 'That order matters' invites the reader to fill in the why — works for both parents and clinicians.
items.sensitivity_flag: 'Upstream/downstream' implies causation; the study shows predictive relationship after controlling for anxiety, which supports the framing but doesn't prove causation. The language is directional rather than absolute — acceptable, but worth a second read against the primary source.

items.text: Remote work was never a perk for many autistic and ADHD workers. It was a de facto accommodation. RTO mandates are revoking it without going through any accommodation process.
items.rationale: Shifts the RTO debate from preference/culture to access/rights without being combative. Gives neurodivergent workers concrete language for what's actually at stake.

items.text: Late diagnosis brings relief. It also brings grief, and they don't cancel each other out. Part of what you're mourning is who you had to become to survive without a map for 30 or 40 years.
items.rationale: Names the coexistence of relief and grief without artificially resolving it. 'Who you had to become' is the specific, less-named layer — the grief about the adaptive self, not just the missed diagnosis.

items.text: Body doubling isn't a weird workaround. A 2025 VR study found ADHD participants finished tasks 27–30% faster with someone present. External social presence fills the self-activation gap the brain can't reliably fill alone.
items.rationale: Leads with permission, delivers the data, names the mechanism. Converts embarrassment about needing someone in the room into understanding. Immediately usable.
items.sensitivity_flag: The 27–30% figure is cited in Simply Psychology 2026 summarizing the VR study — verify against the primary source before posting.

items.text: 'I can only focus if someone's in the room' isn't a character flaw. It's your nervous system borrowing a regulatory signal it can't reliably generate on its own.
items.rationale: Evergreen shame-removal post built on the body-doubling mechanism. No stat required — the framing does the work. Runs well independently or as a complement to post 8.

items.text: 81% of neurodivergent employees mask at work. The intervention target isn't the employee. It's managers who inadvertently enforce neurotypical performance norms — like treating eye contact as proof of engagement.
items.rationale: Stat as entry point, immediate pivot to structural. The concrete example (eye contact) makes it legible to neurotypical allies and gives managers something specific to examine.

items.text: Psychological safety has to come before disclosure — not the other way around. What would that actually look like in your workplace?
items.rationale: Opens the structural conversation without demanding an answer. The question is genuinely open and invites employers, managers, and HR to think rather than defend. Short, clean, genuinely discussable.

items.text: There's a lot written on low-demand parenting for PDA kids. Almost nothing on doing it as a neurodivergent parent who's already in burnout. Who's regulating *your* nervous system?
items.rationale: Names a gap that exists in lived experience but not yet in published writing. No prescription — just the missing question. The closing line is the whole post. Should generate significant recognition in AuDHD parent communities.
